These are aggregate counts, not a record of individual routes. Follow each ribbon through class, sex and survival; inspect a ribbon to read its count.

```chart

title: Survival differed across class and sex
data: { csv: data/titanic.csv }
encoding: { dimensions: [class, sex, survived], y: people }
axes:
  y: { label: People }
```

*Source: Titanic passenger and crew counts from the British Board of Trade inquiry, via Dawson (1995) and the [R datasets package](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/Titanic.html). Age groups are summed in this view.*

## Class and sex

Seven in ten women aboard survived, and two in ten men. Class mattered within each sex: 97% of the women in first class survived and 46% of those in third. Sex mattered more than class: women in third class survived more often than men in first, of whom 34% did. Men in second class fared worst of all, at 14%.

```chart
type: bar
title: Women survived more often than men in every class
subtitle: Share of each group that survived, adults and children together
data:
  inline:
    - { class: 1st, sex: Women, share: 0.97 }
    - { class: 1st, sex: Men, share: 0.34 }
    - { class: 2nd, sex: Women, share: 0.88 }
    - { class: 2nd, sex: Men, share: 0.14 }
    - { class: 3rd, sex: Women, share: 0.46 }
    - { class: 3rd, sex: Men, share: 0.17 }
    - { class: Crew, sex: Women, share: 0.87 }
    - { class: Crew, sex: Men, share: 0.22 }
encoding: { x: class, y: share, color: sex }
axes:
  y: { label: Survived, format: percent, min: 0, max: 1 }
style: { ratio: "2:1" }
```

*Source: the first chart's counts; survivors divided by those aboard in each group, in whole per cent. Women and men include girls and boys.*

```table
title: Aboard and survived, by class
data:
  inline:
    - { class: First class, aboard: 325, survived: 203, share: "62%" }
    - { class: Second class, aboard: 285, survived: 118, share: "41%" }
    - { class: Third class, aboard: 706, survived: 178, share: "25%" }
    - { class: Crew, aboard: 885, survived: 212, share: "24%" }
    - { class: All, aboard: 2201, survived: 711, share: "32%" }
columns:
  - { key: class, label: Class }
  - { key: aboard, label: Aboard, format: number, align: right }
  - { key: survived, label: Survived, format: number, align: right }
  - { key: share, label: Share, align: right }
```

*Source: the first chart's counts.*

The crew's share, 24%, is close to third class's 25%, for a different reason: 862 of the 885 crew were men. Of the 23 women in the crew, 20 survived.

```table
title: Share that survived, of the women and of the men in each class
data:
  inline:
    - { class: First class, women: "97% of 145", men: "34% of 180" }
    - { class: Second class, women: "88% of 106", men: "14% of 179" }
    - { class: Third class, women: "46% of 196", men: "17% of 510" }
    - { class: Crew, women: "87% of 23", men: "22% of 862" }
    - { class: All, women: "73% of 470", men: "21% of 1,731" }
columns:
  - { key: class, label: Class }
  - { key: women, label: Women, align: right }
  - { key: men, label: Men, align: right }
```

*Source: the first chart's counts. Women and men include girls and boys.*

## The children

The table counts 109 children, all of them passengers, and 57 of them survived. Where they travelled decided most of it.

```callout
kind: neutral
title: Every child in first and second class survived.
body: All 30 did. In third class 27 of 79 children survived, about one in three.
```

```table
title: Children aboard and survived, by class
data:
  inline:
    - { class: First class, aboard: 6, survived: 6, share: "100%" }
    - { class: Second class, aboard: 24, survived: 24, share: "100%" }
    - { class: Third class, aboard: 79, survived: 27, share: "34%" }
    - { class: All, aboard: 109, survived: 57, share: "52%" }
columns:
  - { key: class, label: Class }
  - { key: aboard, label: Children, align: right }
  - { key: survived, label: Survived, align: right }
  - { key: share, label: Share, align: right }
```

*Source: the age split of `data/titanic.csv`, which the first chart sums. The table does not state the age at which a child counts as an adult.*

## What an aggregate hides

- **Counts, not journeys.** These ribbons are counts from a contingency table. They do not trace individuals.
- **Class includes the crew.** The fourth class in the data is the crew, who were aboard to work. Their share is not comparable with a passenger class without that in mind.
- **Small groups make round shares.** Six children travelled first class. 100% of six is a fact about six people.
- **One table among several.** Other tallies of those aboard and lost differ a little from these. This report keeps to the inquiry's counts as Dawson published them.

## Data

`data/titanic.csv` and the photograph travel with the report; `media/SOURCES.md` says where the photograph comes from. The CSV holds 32 rows, one for each combination of class, sex, age group and outcome, with the number of people in it. Every figure in this report is a sum or a share of those rows.
